title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma Retreat 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Bodhi Pakshika Dharma, a set of Buddhist lists of practices for being free in the middle of whatever is happening, and gives a quick tour of the whole chart. Nomon explains concentration through a darkened theater, where awareness is a spotlight and mindfulness is remembering that hands rest on the controls. Next comes the Buddha's formula "When this is, that is," set beside Jain, Brahmin, and caste-based views of causality. Nomon then reads from Thanissaro Bhikkhu's The Wings of Awakening about six animals tied together and dragged around until they are tethered to a post, which stands for mindfulness of the body. The Q&A ends with a participant asking how to be of help to Jim, a bitter, ranting brother-in-law.

sentences.text: Welcome, if you're just joining us this morning.
Nice to see you.
We're trying to do this sort of monthly Saturday morning program, more or less, with meditation and a talk.
Often we also include some tea and cookies, but I'm sorry we don't have tea and cookies today.
We're in the middle of a retreat, so we're kind of weaving things together, but glad you could come.
We're trying to take up the possibility of being free, being free in the middle of whatever is happening.
Last night we were saying that there seems to be a huge difference, and it's funny, just like one word different is so enormous, it has such big implications for our life.
We were thinking about the difference between being free from something, free from something, as opposed to being free in something, to be free in the middle of something.

We're taking up sort of one of many Buddhist lists of practices, sets of practices that the Buddha assures us from his diamond seat two thousand five hundred years ago, or maybe it was yesterday, will be helpful in this investigation: how can we be free in the middle of something?
Don't we want to sort of manipulate things and make things better?
Of course we do, but we've seen I think there are limits to that project, some real limits to that approach.
You can only sort of clean things up so much.
I just want to mention I'm using a sort of Sanskrit title for this list of lists, so they might like to know what that means.
It's pretty pedestrian actually, but it sounds impressive, so that gives us some oomph.
To do something impressive is good for us, or maybe not.
The name of this list of lists that we're studying is Bodhi Pakshika Dharma.
Bodhi means waking up, to awaken.
Throughout most world religions, they use some metaphors around sleeping and waking, around light and dark, and I think that's really quite universal.
Bodhi is waking up, like waking up in the morning, or waking up in some more sort of fundamental way to what's actually happening, not being asleep, not sleeping through our life.
Pakshika, I think, is just an ordinary word; it means things that relate to something, things relating to.
So Bodhi, awakening, so things that relate to awakening.
Dharma has a great double meaning, or maybe triple meaning, which I'll talk about a lot, but it's important though.
On the one hand, Dharma means the teachings of Buddha or just teachings in general.
When the monks wandered around India looking for different teachers, they could ask, "What is your teacher's Dharma?"
"What is your teacher's Dharma?"
"What is their teaching?"
That's usually written in English with a capital D.
But then Dharma also actually means like experience itself, like a moment or an instant of experience.
What is the Dharma arising right now?
They had various ways of classifying and understanding and studying experience on a very sort of minute, detailed level.
They were sort of like scientists of their own experience.
Our science is kind of from the outside in, using tools to make observations, and this science was kind of from the inside out.
It's interesting that now we seem to more or less in contemporary culture have both working together, which is maybe the best.
It's interesting that it's the same word that these teachings that will help us with freedom are somehow anonymous with our actual experience, our actual life.
There's a teaching right there: we have such a strong tendency to look for something outside to bring something more in or to get something away, freedom from.
This is saying, well, actually the teaching is right in the middle of experience, somehow.
Does everyone have a handout?
This is a handout, not so formal.
We have a handout.
Maybe if anyone doesn't have a handout, someone can bring you one.
There are two handouts, but you have both of them, I guess.
They're in the back.
There's a single kind of double-sided sheet, which is in the form of a ceremony, and then there's two pages stapled together, which is kind of a chart.
Here we can be looking at the ceremony page or just listening; either way is fine, just to get kind of a visual read on the extent of this.
We did a little ceremony last night, which people told me was helpful.
I hope not too exhausting.
It warms you up, though, right?
There are four foundations of mindfulness, something about mindfulness or minding or paying attention to, and those are listed off.
Some of these are my own kind of take on the traditional translation, a little different from usual if you've studied this before.
It mentions the body.
It mentions sensations and reactions, so something about our sensory world and how we react to things.

It mentions thought and emotion, which is interesting because sometimes we might think that spirituality or Buddhism in particular is sort of like about getting rid of thought or something, or like neutralizing emotion.
It mentions thought and emotion, and it mentions patterns, patterns and habits, right?
We all have highly patterned lives with many habits, and so maybe there's a way to practice with that.
Again, big dharma and little dharma right together.
Maybe our bad habits are Buddha in some way, or maybe not; we'll find out.
This is like a little bit of an overview.
Then there's a list of four things which actually kind of work in tandem with the first list, something about the way things arise.
There's a dichotomy in the second list called the four proper exertions.
It talks about unwholesome states and wholesome states, and we'll talk more about that a little later.
It's about feeling into how do we work with what arises and is it somehow harmful or somehow beneficial?
This gets a little tricky because we have so many different ways we sort things, right?
Good, evil, good, bad, like it, don't like it.
The Buddhist seems to be suggesting that we can use that sorting in a skillful way that might help us.
These English words, of course, are not used in Sanskrit and Pali.
It's a choice to use unwholesome and wholesome.
Sometimes skillful and unskillful are used, and once in a while I see an old translation that says good or evil.
We go, "Oh, good and evil."
I'm done with that.
Maybe that's good, too; I'd be a little bit shocked.
We start with sort of areas of mindfulness, of focus maybe, and then ways of working with different states.
Then we seem to take a little tangent here, and it says four bases of freedom.
It has the word concentration repeated in each of the four bases of freedom.
Concentration is a little difficult choice in English because it's used two different ways when translating Buddhism.
The usual way, which is not this one, is concentrating the mind in some way, sort of stabilizing the mind.

I've lately concocted a metaphor, which I told the other night, so some of us will hear it again, that you could think about your life as if you're sitting in a darkened theater, in the back row, probably.
You don't want to be too close to the stage in the back row.
You're sitting in the back row of a darkened theater, and the play is going on, right?
The play is your life.
You're so absorbed, this is happening and that's happening, terrible, oh, great, you know.
You're sort of focusing on one part of the stage and another part of the stage as different sort of dramas, right?
We use the word drama, right?
So dramas are playing out.
This is your life, right?
You may actually even forget that you're sitting in the theater because you get so absorbed.
That's true, like the movies, good theater, like you're so absorbed, you don't even know you're there anymore, right?
You're in the actors, you're in the action and all this.
This happens to us.
One of the things they use in the theater to help sort of direct our attention is lighting, right?
Sometimes only part of the stage is lit, and so we focus on that and we forget the rest of the stage is there, and then they're changing the set or something.
I have this metaphor for how our minds work, which is like the spotlight that they use in the theater.
That little circle of light that the spotlight is shining, that's what we're aware of, right?
We have something that we're aware of in any given moment, and that's what's coming into our consciousness.
A lot of things are happening we're not aware of, right?
Or not consciously aware of.
One way we know that this is true is the way we can do things without remembering we've done them, right?
Like you walk from here to there or even drive from here and there.
It's amazing, like where there are no more accidents and you don't remember, or like you're meant to go somewhere and you end up at home.
Have you ever done that?
So clearly you are not consciously aware of where you're going, right?
And yet the car didn't crash, at least as far as you can tell.
You kind of look at the car and go, "It looks okay," probably wouldn't have noticed, you know.
So there's this little circle of awareness on the play of our life.
When that circle moves around, this is like focus, right?
The awareness gets moved around.
It's like the ability of the mind to focus on one thing or another thing.
Maybe when you were driving, not knowing where you were going, the mind was focusing on a memory or a plan or something like this, but it was focused on something.
Something was happening; you're aware of something.
We have the ability consciously to move the focus around, right?
To some extent.
You may be attempting to focus on my words right now, but maybe you just move somewhere else.
Are you back?
That happens, right?
We have some conscious ability to move awareness, which is focus.
So awareness and focus.
Then mindfulness.
This is the point of all this.
Mindfulness is when you suddenly remember not only are you sitting there in the back of the house, but you're sitting right in front of the spotlight; it turns out.
And actually your hands are on the controls.
You just didn't notice, you know.
So you're like, "Oh, you know, I can, I have a little more ability here to manipulate or kind of be aware of the process of how the focus and the awareness are moving around."
I can deliberately bring my attention back, right?
That's like meditation.
It's like, "Oh yeah, bring the attention back, bring the attention back, bring it back."
Mindfulness is just the remembering actually.
The root word that's being translated, its first meaning is memory for mindfulness, so I'm coming around to concentration.
Concentration, one meaning of concentration, it's just developing the ability to have your hands be a little steadier on the controls there, you know?
Just a little steadier.
But when we say concentration in English, we tend to picture Rodin's like the thinker, right?
Or Pascal, you know, or Descartes, or these characters who are such important people in our intellectual history, really smart people.
Oh man, it turns out, I guess, there must have been really smart women thinking about these things too.
In Western thought, we think of concentration as a very narrow focus.

Then you realize, with our spotlight, we can have a really narrow beam just on one little idea or one thought, or like solving a math problem, or, unfortunately for us, one really nasty personality trait or one really troublesome thing that's happening in the world or in our life, right?
So we think concentration is a very narrow focus.
But actually, the way concentration is understood here is it's just a steadiness.
The focus could be really narrow.
The focus could be really broad.
It could be like wide open, allowing the whole of experience to just come in, your eyes wide open.

Everything's happening on the stage, and you feel the house, and you feel the chair, and you're aware of the other people in the house, but you're just steady with that awareness, not like, you know, steady.
So it seems like there can be a narrowness of focus, a little teeny circle of awareness, or a great big circle of awareness.
We can also be deliberate, mindfulness remembering, that we can also aim and we can focus this spotlight.
Concentration is a steadiness, usually, but this one in the list here called the Four Bases of Freedom is not that.
That's coming later.
I just wanted to explicate that a little bit.
This is like concentration, like concentrating things, like making them very dense and strong and powerful.

This is going to be really interesting to talk about because last night we talked about the sort of hazards of the way the mind is constantly generating desire for things to be a little bit different from where they are, the way they are, or a lot different.

We talked about a traditional Buddhist list of sort of the root problem in mind, according to Buddhism, is this sort of one of these lists of the root problem, originally translated as greed, hatred, and delusion, and maybe I was saying a helpful translation for these three thrust of mind might be desire, annoyance, and ignorance, or confusion as a possibility.
What you notice about number nine, maybe, is there's the word desire.
That's interesting.
It might be that there's skillful desire or wholesome desire and unskillful or unwholesome desire.
Well, yeah, there is.
It might be.
So yeah, some way of working with desire that's helpful, so we'll get to that.
This is the big picture here.
There's something about persistence and intention and discrimination, so applying some tools here.

What's interesting is that we have a sort of wing of Buddhist practice and understanding that's emphasized in the Zen school around just radical acceptance and just being, just being in the middle of what is.
That's really true; we need that.
Then also, here are a set of tools, here are a set of tools that maybe we can work with at what's just happening in creative ways to support the ability to have freedom in, to have freedom in.
Then we have some repeats.
Did you notice that?
Have you looked at this list yet?
The five wholesome roots, my translation, and the five wholesome strengths are the same words repeated: faith, faith, yeah, faith, diligence.
There's mindfulness again in another context.
And this, and actually here I have a difference and it's a mistake, but I decided to leave it in.
Number 16, the five wholesome roots, I left in the word, I put in the word concentration.
So that's that steadiness on the controls, just being able to be steady with what's happening—maybe narrow, maybe broad focus.
But actually the word that's being translated there is the Sanskrit, I think it's the same in Pali, word *samadhi*.
And see, in the second list of repeats, number 21, I left it with the Sanskrit word.
And that's kind of to remind us that we don't mean exactly this kind of Western idea of like thinking really hard, crunching up our brow and figuring something out.
*Samadhi* has both this quality of steady openness to reality and it also has some connotations for developing meditation practice.
So we'll get into that later.
There are some specifics in Buddhist meditation psychology, if you will, around *samadhi* that is both steadiness and it's cultivating some depth in meditation.
And then we have wisdom.
And again, wisdom has a little different flavor in Buddhism than in Western thought, so that'll be interesting to see.
I don't know how much of all this we'll have time to explore; some of this we may take up five years from now.
Remember that?
And then continuing our global tour, our light speed tour through the practice of the lifetime here, we have seven factors of enlightenment, or sometimes they say awakening.

And probably awakening is better, but I learned it so much as factors of enlightenment I couldn't get myself to change it because enlightenment's a little bit of trouble for us, because we may think there's some special better state that we'll get sometime, or maybe we despair that we'll never get sometime.
It's called enlightenment.
And there do seem to be some subtle or not so subtle state changes that happen over years of practice, not to say that there aren't.
But our obsession with things being very concrete and state-oriented just basically messes us up more than it helps us, so better to think of all this as process.
And awakening is probably a better word than enlightenment, or maybe we should say enlightening—the sense that we fall asleep, we wake up.
We fall asleep, we wake up, and we have this sort of big vow to just keep waking up, just keep waking up.
So enlightenment sounds like you're done or something like this, but maybe later we might change it anyway, but I couldn't do it.
And then we have another list of qualities.
And we've seen mindfulness before, we've seen discernment before, we've seen diligent before, but then look at 26 and 27: joy and lightness and ease.
So we shouldn't have to be too dour about this project of freedom; this should be fun.
It should be fun to be a little more free in the middle of our life to get to enjoy our experience, even when it's not what we ordered or not what we wanted.
But there's a kind of joyfulness even in the middle of trouble and a little trouble maybe in the middle of joyfulness, but that's another story.
So there's joy and lightness and ease.

Then we have again *samadhi* or concentration, and then we have equanimity, which is another way of talking about sort of stableness and steadiness, not knocked over, not knocked over by the winds of our life.
And that equanimity is something we practice very physically in the Zen tradition—very physical practice of equanimity.
That's why we don't move, that's why we don't move.
You may have thought it was because we're tough or something, but not at all.

We move because we practice the possibility of allowing something to arise in our experience and to just be with it, just be with it without reaction, without jumping up, without changing our posture, without scratching that itch.
Just be with itchiness, be with peacefulness.
And internally, same thing.
Even when things, maybe we're so lucky to have a very pleasant experience that we enjoy during meditation, so not to be sort of grabbing onto that, to be equanimous with whatever our experience is.
So equanimity is something we practice very directly.
And then the Eightfold Noble Path is one of the most famous lists in Buddhism, so you've probably seen this before.
And so I think I won't mention it now, but many of the words that we saw earlier are repeated again.
So it's the same thing, but different in each case—maybe a different slant or a different angle on these different practices and qualities of mind and heart.
So there's intention again, mindfulness and *samadhi* are there again.
Right effort is actually often described in total by the second list, back to the four proper exertions.
And I listened to Edie give a talk on the Eightfold Noble Path this last summer, and I noticed she mentioned those as a description of right effort; it's what's usually mentioned.
And this last list is interesting too, because it folds this whole thing right out of the meditation hall too.
It reminds us this is about our entire life.
What work do we do?
Right livelihood?
How do we talk?

The wonderful thing about a formal meditation retreat is you can sometimes take a break from the challenge of speech, and in this retreat we're doing a little bit talking, a little bit not talking, but of course we're always talking, so to include that as practice.
And number 30 is maybe what makes this whole entire thing unfold in a beneficial way, instead of a difficult, another failed project kind of way: just what is our view?
What is our view?
And Buddha saw this as very important.

And I think in Western thought we don't see our view as that important because we posit an external reality that's sort of objective, and our subjective view is just sort of trying to look at that objective view.
But the Buddha kind of flipped around the other way; he felt the way you view reality and your life creates your life, and creates reality in a very real way.
So how you look at things is very important.
So there's a little overview of this Bodhi Paksika Dharma.
And now let's set that aside and let me just say a few things about, not too many things, about some of the underlying thought that maybe the Buddha brought or the Buddha's tradition.
And you know when I say the Buddha, it's kind of like shorthand, you know, shorthand for two thousand five hundred years of many thousands of men and women trying to practice and understand this.
We don't actually know, of course, what the Buddha said two thousand five hundred years ago.
I mentioned last night we don't even know when he lived exactly, I think we're pretty good on where he lived.
So when he gave these teachings they weren't written down anywhere; they were recorded much, much later.

So one thing I think that scholars pretty well agree on is that in the Buddha's day it was a very rich time in terms of thinking about what causes things to happen, what causes things to happen or not happen.
And I think all of us have a well-developed theory of our own of causality.
We don't think about it too much, but we have an idea like this leads to that, right?
That doesn't lead to that.
And one of the great causes of our suffering is when it doesn't seem to go the way we thought it was supposed to go, right?
Or when some other person seems to have the temerity to think that their theory of causality is right and ours is wrong, right?

So I think scholars agree that there was a rich time in the fifth or sixth century before the Common Era of India in thinking about causality, and that the Buddha kind of put together a very fairly, more or less new spin on causality that's really important to us.

So I'm already using more time than I plan to, but I'll attempt to say a little bit about that because it's hard to think about this stuff because our view is quite ingrained, quite habitual, and so therefore it's hard to talk about it in a helpful way.

So one way that we all kind of have heard about about the Indian caste system, it's a little bit stereotyped, but I think it's somewhat true, that one view at the time was that your actions in this life don't make much difference in this life; they will benefit you in the next life.
And so they have a system of rebirth and levels, people occupy different levels in society.

And this seems to have been in some ways very reassuring and peaceful, creating a very ordered society, and in other ways like the most smartest political repression you ever could have invented, you know, that the people in the top caste could encourage the people in the lower caste to be content with their lot and hope for a better rebirth.

But that's part of the background of Buddhist thought, that there are effects far into the future from our actions, in another life even, but maybe, you know, in one case not so much what's happening now.
So sort of a long view of cause and effect.

There was another view that was the practice, I think, I don't know that much about it, but the practice of another religion that was contemporaneous with Buddhism, which is the religion of the Jains.
The Jains went the other way.
They said, well, actually, every present moment action you take has enormous consequences, and so they were very literal in their practice of morality and care.
And they tried very hard not to harm any other beings.
They would filter their water to avoid harming invisible beings.
I don't know if they had the idea of microbes in, I think they were like the first fruititarians.

And the ultimate sort of practice of Jains was to live such a quiet, non-harming, this is *Ahimsa*, right, non-harming life that the ideal of practice was just to kind of quietly starve yourself to death.
I don't know how many of them actually did that, so they wouldn't harm anybody.
It was like the ultimate in religious purity and practice.
So that's like present moment: present action is very effective because they felt like if you step on a bug, it rocks the world in a certain way and causes enormous harm.
So that's important to think about: what happens now matters.

And then there's another line of thought, which is kind of a hybrid between the two, which is the way of thinking of the Brahmins, the sort of priestly class that had sort of grown up to dominate the society only, I think, a few hundred years before the Buddha.
We think of it as this long, long thing, but I think it was a little more recent.
And the Brahmin theory was that the only effective action were Brahmin ritual actions.
So if you want things to go better, you need a Brahmin to do a special ritual that has positive effects.
You want to have a good harvest, you need to hire a Brahmin.
You're wishing or you're plowing the fields carefully or the rain or something like that was much less important.
More important was the effectiveness of Brahmin rituals.
And you can see the social effects of that.
So the Buddha kind of rolled all this together in a really helpful way for us.
And shoot, I'm not going to get to what I want to get to.
So I had this huge anxiety last week that I wasn't going to have anything to say, just to show what we know.
I was really stressed out about it.
I didn't have much time to prepare, you know.
Good thing.
So the Buddha had the idea that what's happening now matters in a certain way, and what happened in the past matters in a certain way.
And when I talked about the earlier ones, they were looking forward and past, like previous lives would affect this life, right?
And so this was his formulation of this, and it's written in such a simple way, it's deceptively simple.
I don't know if you can all see this.
I'll read it out loud: *When this is, that is.
Part one.
When this is, that is.
Part two.
From the arising of this comes the arising of that.
So from the arising of this comes the arising of that.
So these are causal links.*
And then the opposite: *When this isn't, that isn't.
When this isn't, that isn't.* Two things can't arise together or can't exist together somehow.
Sorry.

And the last one is: *From the stopping of this comes the stopping of that.* So the first and third are about present moment—the idea that some things sort of tend to exist together have sort of a positive effect on each other: *When this is, that is.* That's the first.
And the third is that the opposite can also be true: some things when they're present, some other thing is not present.
This is quite abstract, so we have to work up to kind of chew on this I think before it's useful.
And then the second and fourth are more about the past and future.
So something arises conditioned by something in the past probably, and as it arises it encourages something else to arise, sort of linking things together.
And then the opposite: something can stop, no longer be arising, and then some other thing that somehow is linked to it doesn't arise anymore.
And I think one way to think about all this, I don't want to spend another hour on it, I'm tempted, but I won't.
One way to think about it is kind of this way.
Let's say that we're kind of here.
Show my drawing: little smile, maybe half smile.
And let's say that the past is below us.
I think we tend to visualize the past as below us, not like the past as a direction.
So conditioning from the past is kind of always coming up—our history, our patterns, our habits, and it can go really far back: how we were raised, how our parents were raised, and back and back.
There's all this sort of conditioning arising, and what that conditioning from the past is meeting is the present moment.
So then at the same time, let's put all this in both directions: there's present moment experience, and these two things are interacting in a very complicated and interesting way.
So this kind of helps us to understand on the one hand, everything is not preordained.
We're here, we're right in the middle of this present experience.
We have choices: we can say this or say that.
We can take this action or that action.
And in the third case here, that's going to have a very real effect.
If we choose this, then maybe that is somehow connected to it, or we choose not to do this, some other thing doesn't happen.
So we have some choice.
At the same time, flooding into these choice points, this experience, this perception, and this view, right.
All this that's coming in is affecting how we think, how we view, and how we understand, and sort of like what we think is actually happening.
All that is being strongly influenced by the past.
In Buddhist cosmology, that would even include past lives.
So we're kind of standing at this junction all the time.
And where it gets interesting is each of us is standing at a slightly different junction.
Like here's our friend over here, right?
So to some extent, they're participating in the same reality as us in this present moment, right?
But let's give them another color.
A whole different set of conditioning, personality, history, whatever you want to call it, is arising for our friend.
So they're sort of in our world and in a different world at the same time.
So that, I think, was kind of the Buddha's genius here.

One way you could express this, which I remember one of my favorite phrases from my teacher Norman Fischer, which one of you that I remember, is he said for a while he was saying this whole kind of thing of your life, it's not your fault.
It's not your fault.
You didn't, you know.
It's not your fault.
But it's your responsibility.
Your responsibility.
You're here, right at that, you're the one at that junction.
You're the one at that junction with the possibility of taking a weekend retreat and practicing these things.
And yet, your failings and your limitations and the momentum and the mistakes, not exactly your fault either.

And yet, as things rise up from the past and enter into the future and enter into this and that world that we're in the middle of, our responsibility to work with it as best we can for the welfare of all beings, as the Buddha was telling us last night.
I was going to talk about the body a little bit.
Then I'll stop.
Maybe we have questions.
So it starts with the body, number one.
Number one is the body.
So I think this is like hard to underestimate how important this is to us.
Because we kind of like living up here, right?
Oh, it's about the mind.
I just sort of figured it out.
I thought about it in the right way.
I would be happier.
The Buddha is saying, well, not so fast.
What is the feeling in the body?
I have four or five picked out, but I'll just share one of the teachings from the Buddha on this.
Because he emphasizes this a lot more than I do.
I mean, I've been studying mindfulness a lot.
It was really interesting to...
These are from Thanissaro's book on this list, Thanissaro Bhikkhu's book on this list, which he calls *The Wings of Awakening*.
I can bring this up really quickly here.
Yeah, this is really interesting.
I'll tell you the story and then we can have a little bit of discussion and hopefully it won't have us too far past the schedule.
So the Buddha said this.
It is recorded.
There's a case where a monk seeing a form with the eyes is obsessed.
Does this happen to you?
Is obsessed with pleasing forms and is repelled by unpleasing forms and remains with their body mindfulness unestablished.
So just sort of in their heads, you know, excited about this, hating that, with limited awareness.
So there's that case.
He does not discern, as it has come to be, the awareness release, the discernment release, where any evil, unskillful mental qualities that have arisen utterly cease without trace.
So the last one's a little bit coded, but he doesn't know what to do, basically.
He's caught and not aware of the body.
This is just as if a person, catching six animals of different ranges and habitats, were to bind those six animals with a strong rope.
Buddha had great metaphors.
So it's as if catching six different animals, tying them together.
Catching a snake, who would bind it with a strong rope.
Catching a crocodile, a bird, a dog, a hyena, and a monkey.
Bind all these together.
They're all tied together.
Binding them all with a strong rope, and tying a knot in the middle, he would chase them.
So this is as if you tie those animals together, and you tie them together, and you're like, trying to keep up with them.
Those six animals of their different ranges and habitats, and habits, would all pull towards their own place.
The snake would pull, thinking, I'll go to the anthill.
The crocodile would pull, thinking, I'll go into the water.
